pages.title: Title
pages.summary: The value premium.

pages.title: Roadmap
pages.summary: LSV 1994 (behavioral), FF 1996 (risk), DT 1997 (characteristics vs covariances), the replies (DFF 2000, Berk 2001), and value 1990–today. Running question: risk premium or persistent mistake?

pages.title: Value and growth: the basic sort
pages.summary: Value = high B/M, C/P, E/P; glamour = low. Cheap beats expensive ≈10%/yr before risk adjustment. LSV: extrapolation error; FF: distress risk; DT: a test to break the tie.

pages.title: LSV thesis
pages.summary: Overreaction/extrapolation: crowds stampede into glamour (depressing future returns), over-punish value. And NOT riskier: no higher variance, betas, downside, or bad-state underperformance.

pages.title: Making it testable
pages.summary: Split PAST growth (realized sales/earnings/CF growth) from EXPECTED future growth (multiples E/P, C/P). Risk requires value to underperform with frequency in high-marginal-utility states.

pages.title: Data & methodology
pages.summary: NYSE-AMEX 1963–90 (strategies from 1968), EW annual buy-and-hold t+1..t+5. Delisting → size-decile replacement. Selection traps: COMPUSTAT back-fill, delisting returns cluster in distressed value names — biases run AGAINST finding the premium.

pages.title: Measuring growth
pages.summary: Portfolio earnings yield with $1 weights; average over time FIRST then compute growth (AE ratios) so negative earnings don't explode the rate. Sales growth (GS) as the steadier past-growth ranking.

pages.title: Expected growth via Gordon
pages.summary: P=D/(r−g): holding r fixed, high price vs fundamentals (low C/P, E/P) ⟹ market expects high g. Multiples proxy expected growth; alternative: analyst forecasts (La Porta 1993).

pages.title: The refined strategy: Table II Panel A
pages.summary: Double sort C/P × GS. Glamour corner (low C/P, high GS) 11.3%/yr; value corner 21.5% — 10.2-pt spread, wider than any one-way sort.

pages.title: Table II Panels D & E
pages.summary: Without GS: E/P×B/M 18.9 vs 11.6 (7.3); B/M×C/P 19.4 vs 11.1 (8.3). The spread is everywhere.

pages.title: Robustness
pages.summary: Survives within size groups; selection biases push against it; Fama–MacBeth (Table IV): C/P t≈3.7–4.6, GS t≈−2.1 to −2.8 keep independent power; B/M and SIZE fade once C/P and GS are in.

pages.title: Expectations are wrong (Table V)
pages.summary: Glamour's priced-in growth advantage fades by years 3–5 — the extrapolated persistence never materializes. Slow-motion correction: the mirror image of momentum.

pages.title: Value wins when it counts (Figure 2)
pages.summary: Annual value−glamour 1968–89: positive in ≥17/22 years and every 5-year window; holds in NBER recessions (R) and market-decline years (D). Real bar data embedded in the deck.

pages.title: So is it risk? No
pages.summary: No higher betas/SDs; no bad-state underperformance. ICAPM lens motivates the test; the APT door (an unnamed priced factor) is left open — FF96 walk through it.

pages.title: Why a free premium survives
pages.summary: Individuals confuse good companies with good investments; institutions prefer defensible glamour; horizons too short for multi-year convergence. Data-mining defenses: international and pre-sample evidence.

pages.title: FF96: the three-factor model
pages.summary: E[r]=rf+b·MKT+s·SMB+h·HML. Claim: one model absorbs (almost) every CAPM anomaly — consistent with ICAPM/APT. Holdout: momentum.

pages.title: HML as distress
pages.summary: Weak/low-earnings firms have high h; value = fallen angels with more distress exposure ⟹ premium is a wage. FF96 extends FF93 to the E/P, C/P, sales-growth (LSV) sorts and DeBondt–Thaler reversal.

pages.title: It explains the value sorts
pages.summary: Three-factor alphas ≤9bp/mo across B/M, E/P, C/P, past-return deciles; GRS fails to reject: E/P p=0.59, C/P p=0.90, 5-yr reversal p=0.56. The 25 size-B/M sorts reject only because R²>93% makes tiny alphas detectable.

pages.title: …even the LSV double sorts
pages.summary: On LSV's own refined sorts: GRS p=0.28 (B/M), 0.39 (E/P), 0.41 (C/P). The model passes its adversary's test.

pages.title: The one failure: momentum
pages.summary: t−12:t−2 sort: GRS 4.45, p=0.000 — rejected. Losers load HIGH on s and h (small/distressed/value-like) so the model predicts high returns; they earn low. Longer horizons recover (t−48:t−2 p=0.031; t−60:t−13 p=0.235).

pages.title: MMV interpretation
pages.summary: The factors are ~multifactor-minimum-variance; any three spanning portfolios price identically (Tables VIII–IX). SMB/HML chosen for near-zero correlation (interpretability), not uniqueness.

pages.title: Spanning regressions
pages.summary: S, L, H on market alone: R² 0.79–0.92; on each other: 0.98–0.99. The 3-factor SPACE matters, not the construction.

pages.title: Scorecard across specs
pages.summary: Five 3-factor specifications give nearly identical average |a| per test set; momentum rejected under every one (p=0.000).

pages.title: Is it actually risk?
pages.summary: In favor: real common covariation, factors in fundamentals too. Unfinished: name the state variable, explain the special premium; distress is not macro-correlated — convenient and awkward.

pages.title: FF push back on behavioral
pages.summary: HML Sharpe not exceptional (H underperforms L about as often as small vs big, market vs bills); the premium persists ≥5 years while the earnings mean-reversion LSV cite happens sooner.

pages.title: Data mining check
pages.summary: VW NYSE-based factors limit survivor bias; Davis 1994 pre-1962 and international evidence are true out-of-sample; the unification itself argues against many independent flukes. Roll's proxy caveat remains.

pages.title: The momentum puzzle stays open
pages.summary: Out-of-sample robust (JT 2000, Rouwenhorst); uncaptured by 3 factors; a challenge to behavioral models too. Post-1990 growth beat value — supports whom?

pages.title: DT: the deeper question
pages.summary: Covariances (how you co-move) or characteristics (what you are)? DT: no pervasive size/B/M factors, no premia on loadings. High-B/M stocks co-moved BEFORE distress (industry/region) — comovement predates the supposed risk. Tests the FF story, not LSV's.

pages.title: Three hypotheses
pages.summary: Model 1: distress factor, constant premia. Model 2: time-varying premia, no distress factor. Model 3: characteristics price directly (implies asymptotic arbitrage). Test 1 kills 1; Test 2 separates 2 from 3.

pages.title: Test 1: pre/post SD
pages.summary: Portfolio return SDs barely change as firms become high/low B/M — the covariation is persistent (industry/region), not switched on by distress. Inconsistent with model 1.

pages.title: Test 2: the clever sort
pages.summary: Sort on characteristics (size, B/M) first, then WITHIN groups on pre-formation HML loading (t−42..t−7, portfolios to tame EIV). Model 2: returns rise with loading. Model 3: flat. 1973–93, all exchanges.

pages.title: Result: covariances don't price
pages.summary: Average returns across loading quintiles: 0.740, 0.817, 0.846, 0.866, 0.806 — flat. Characteristics win.

pages.title: Caveats
pages.summary: Characteristic may proxy an unknown true factor; betas measured with error vs characteristics measured without (mechanical win); time-varying loadings. DT don't claim free lunch — only that FF's distress-factor story fails.

pages.title: The replies
pages.summary: Davis–Fama–French 2000: extend to 1927–97, the DT result disappears. Berk 2001: dependent sorts bias toward the characteristic model; use independent sorts. DT reply: the dependent sort is the only way to hold the characteristic fixed.

pages.title: Why it matters
pages.summary: If characteristics price: benchmark performance on characteristics not loadings; cost of capital depends on what a firm IS; event-study counterfactuals change. Still unsettled.

pages.title: Where the debate stands
pages.summary: LSV behavioral / FF rational / DT characteristics — one robust fact, three readings; momentum troubles everyone.

pages.title: Same trade, two stories
pages.summary: DFA (FF, risk pitch) vs LSV Asset Management (behavioral pitch): value strategies ≈0.98 correlated. The story determines whether clients hold through drawdowns.

pages.title: The 2017–20 drawdown
pages.summary: Deepest/longest value drawdown in ~100 years (back to 1825): HML ≈−50%, Russell −55%, MSCI −54%, AQR −50%. Source: AQR, Is (Systematic) Value Investing Dead? (2020).

pages.title: Drawdown chart
pages.summary: Cumulative value and drawdown, 1990–2023 (AQR hypothetical).

pages.title: Absolute return ≠ all the time
pages.summary: At SR=0.4 you underperform cash ≈34% of years and ≈10% of decades — a multi-year drawdown is statistically ordinary. Value still works across US/Japan/Europe/EM, bonds, currencies.

pages.title: Underperformance-probability chart
pages.summary: P(underperform cash) by horizon for SR 0.4 vs 0.7.

pages.title: The suspects
pages.summary: Structural: deserved cheapness, low rates/QE, FANG winner-take-all, intangibles. Market-structure: buybacks, crowding, wrong measurement. Each is testable.

pages.title: Ruled out
pages.summary: Drop biggest 10%/tech/most-expensive decile — spread barely moves. Drop high-intangibles — still wide. Fundamentals gaps normal. Little recession/crash sensitivity. Rates: correlation rose 0.1→0.5 but explain only 15–30% (Maloney–Moskowitz 2020).

pages.title: FANGs chart
pages.summary: Value spread with/without largest 10%, both near 90th percentile.

pages.title: Rates chart
pages.summary: Value vs 10-yr-yield changes; ≈15% variance explained.

pages.title: The value spread
pages.summary: Expensive basket's multiple / cheap basket's = the value spread. Widening spread IS the drawdown; a wide spread is the recovery setup.

pages.title: Spread chart
pages.summary: By 2020 ≈99th percentile — beyond the 2000 tech-bubble peak.

pages.title: Implied growth dislocation
pages.summary: Justifying the spread requires expensive to out-grow cheap by 80–110% over 5 years — larger than ANY realized differential. LSV extrapolation live; last analog 1999–2000.

pages.title: Implied-growth chart
pages.summary: Implied vs realized expensive−cheap 5-yr growth.

pages.title: The recovery
pages.summary: Post-tech-bubble value returned ≈+75–108%. This recovery began ≈Nov 2020; by 2023–24 spreads still 80th–90th percentile. The spread is the forward-looking instrument both camps watch.

pages.title: Recovery chart
pages.summary: Spread with post-2000 recovery (+93%) annotated.

pages.title: Risk or behavioral, live
pages.summary: Re-pricing character, spread predictability, 1999 echo lean behavioral; but a true premium can go negative for a decade and the spread could be a time-varying price of risk. Data under-determine the why.

pages.title: Talking to investors
pages.summary: Premia have stretches that feel like failure; the spread (not recent returns) is the signal; the premium is earned by staying invested. Same 0.98-correlated trade, two stories — the story decides who holds on.

pages.title: (closing)
pages.summary: Size value so you survive the drawdown; lean in when the spread is wide.
